newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr bulls find some rate relief in data.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr bulls find some rate relief in data.

text.p: The Australian dollar crept higher at the midsession as a firm set of domestic data was taken as slightly reducing the chances of another official rate cut.

Bulls won early relief from rate tenson when the Reserve Bank let its 9.30 am operation pass with no move, confounding those who thought it would cut at the first opportunity following Tuesday's board meeting.

There remained a risk it would move Thursday, but dealers reckoned a reported 2.9 percent rise in May retail sales made that less likely. Sentiment was also underpinned by news from Moody's the outlook for Australia's credit rating was improving.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar had staged a careful rally to US$0.7533/38 having eased to US$0.7510/15 at the opening from US$0.7525/30 late here Tuesday.
Traders said offshore offers were lined up at US$0.7540 and resistance had already proved stiff by capping a jump immediately after the economic figures hit dealing screens.

But, assuming the view the RBA was on hold gained wider acceptance in the market, as most dealers expected, there was a real chance of a break higher and a push to Monday's US$0.7570 peak. Support was seen at US$0.7505 and it would take a breach off US$0.7470 to signal a resumption of the old downtrend.
The dollar had delved as deep as US$0.7440 last Friday, a 17-month low, as the market succumbed to fears the RBA would ease after its monthly board meeting this week.
Sentiment turned just as quickly against a move late on Monday as the dollar rallied over a cent and today's events had merely confirmed that bias, analysts said.
The 2.9 percent jump in retail sales for May was the largest since March 1994 and at the very top end of market forecasts.
Analysts cautioned the data were volatile and it was far too early to say the consumer was regaining confidence, but the rise did at least make up for April's shock 1.7 percent fall.
The strength in May meant sales were up 4.5 percent on the year so far and suggested the economic gloom which descended on the market last month might have been overdone.

The futures market seemed to agree and the 90-day bank bill contract for September dipped six basis points to 94.79. That still implied a rate of 5.21 percent, however, reflecting the belief the 5.50 percent official cash rate could yet be cut.

Analysts were even more ready to entertain an easing and were quick to pick holes in the data saying they were of little significance to the policy outlook. A conclusion which made some dealers wonder why they had been so worried ahead of the data.

A case in point were building approvals figures out today which showed a 2.2 percent rise in May, a relatively firm result on the surface. However, the gain was entirely due to the approval of an Olympic Games housing development which comprised a total of 1,561 new dwellings.
Without that, approvals would have fallen 12 percent on the April level of 12,062.

But the Bureau of Statistics reported that Victoria had been under-reporting approvals for the three months to April which added a total of 1,472 new dwellings to the period. Furthermore, it had conducted an annual seasonal re-analysis of the series.
This had seen approvals estimates revised up further for the February to April period so that March, for instance, now had 12,374 approvals recorded instead of 11,368.
The impact on the past course of monthly changes was quite radical with April approvals now reported to have fallen 2.5 percent against an original 3.9 percent rise.

Elsewhere, the local dollar leapt on the Thai baht in wild trading after the Thai government announced a managed float of the embattled currency. The A$ shot to 21.00 baht in the wake of the decision from 18.30 early this morning.
